brief.from: The previous section finished encode and decode, so any string can become a list of ids and back.

beats.idea: A language model is checked on text it was not trained on, so the single string is cut into two pieces: a large one to learn from and a small one held back.
beats.shows: The learner can state the cut in plain words: first 90% of characters train, last 10% validate.

beats.idea: The cut is plain string slicing at one index; the same index ends the first piece and starts the second, so the pieces share no character and miss none.
beats.shows: The learner points at the two slicing lines and sees the same int(n*0.9) used as end and start.

beats.idea: Worked example with the real numbers: n is 1,115,394, so n*0.9 is 1,003,854.6 and int drops it to 1,003,854.
beats.shows: The learner computes 1,003,854 train characters and 1,115,394 − 1,003,854 = 111,540 validation characters, matching the comments.

beats.idea: The cut is made on the raw text before encoding, then each piece is encoded; for characters, id counts equal slice lengths.
beats.shows: The learner sees the encode lines produce 1,003,854 and 111,540 ids.

beats.idea: The GPT-2 BPE script uses the same two-line split; only the encoder differs, so token counts differ (301,966 and 36,059) while the 90/10 cut is the same.
beats.shows: The learner compares the two scripts' slicing lines side by side.

brief.to: Next: why the held-back tenth must never be seen during training.
